title: The role of percutaneous trans-hepatic and trans-splenic variceal obliteration in uncontrolled gastric variceal bleeding
content:
by Kiyoun Yi, Young Joo Park, Hojun Lee, Hoon Kwon, Hyun Young Woo, Jeong Heo, Chang Won Kim

Background/Aims

Gastric variceal bleeding (GVB) is a serious complication of portal hypertension, with limited therapeutic options when conventional endoscopic and radiologic interventions are not feasible. Percutaneous trans-hepatic and trans-splenic variceal obliteration (PTVO) has been described as a salvage therapy; however, clinical evidence regarding its efficacy and safety remains scarce.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 23 cirrhotic patients (median age, 58 years; 18 men) who underwent PTVO for uncontrolled GVB between October 2017 to July 2024 at a tertiary hospital. Primary endpoints were technical success and postprocedural changes in liver function. Secondary endpoints included complications, length of hospital stay (LOS), rebleeding rates, and survival.

Results

PTVO was technically successful in all patients without procedure-related complications. Hepatic function, which was assessed by Child-Pugh, model for end stage liver disease, and albumin-bilirubin scores, remained stable during 12-month follow-up. The median LOS was 13 days (range, 3–48). During a mean follow-up of 45.6 months, rebleeding occurred in 10 patients (43.5%). Accounting for death as a competing event, the cumulative incidence of rebleeding was 18% at 6 weeks and 22.9% at 1 year. The Kaplan–Meier estimated survival probabilities were 91.1% and 61.1%, respectively.

Conclusions

In this small, retrospective cohort of highly selected patients with uncontrolled GVB for whom conventional treatment options were not feasible, PTVO was technically feasible in all cases. Among patients with available follow-up, no apparent deterioration in liver-function measures was observed. These findings provide preliminary descriptive evidence supporting PTVO as a possible rescue option in this clinical setting.
